gap: No result ChatGPT got says that on the cheap 2000 W hair-dryer combo converters (Ceptics LX2-M2000, TESSAN's 2000W/200W 4-USB unit and BESTEK's 2000W Europe unit) the extra 200 W outlet and the USB ports do not convert voltage, so a 110 V-only US device plugged in there gets the local 220–240 V. Of the units checked, only Ceptics' $129.99 VC-S2000 says both of its outlets support up to 2000 W.
standout_why: I compared against globalplugs.com, cabinandcarry.com, voltwander.com/faq, plugvoltage.com and momax.net; ChatGPT cited none of its results. None of them names a combo converter or says that some of its outlets pass local voltage straight through. Global Plugs says combo adapter-converters are 'typically 25-100 W' and tells readers to 'Avoid them', but the 200–2000 W combos on maker stores today contradict that. Momax says only that a plain universal adapter's AC outlet passes 230 V through. VoltWander says a hair dryer needs a 2000 W+ converter but names no product and doesn't say which outlet converts. ChatGPT's answer showed only two 200–250 W units and told the shopper they can't run a hair dryer. It never mentioned the $46–50 2000 W combos or their dead-voltage outlet.
decides: For phones, a toothbrush or a shaver (under 200–250 W), pick a unit where every AC outlet converts: TESSAN TC03 at $43.99, or Ceptics PU-200C at $34.99 if you only go to 220–240 V countries. For a 120 V-only hair dryer the choice depends on the dryer. If it has a mechanical switch, the $46.99–49.99 combos work, but the US device has to go in the 2000 W outlet, because the 200 W outlet passes 220 V. If it's a Dyson or Shark-style digital dryer, those combos rule it out. Ceptics' VC-S2000 at $129.99 is the only unit checked whose outlets both support 2000 W, but its maker page doesn't say whether it runs digital dryers. Otherwise use a dual-voltage dryer.
